recaps.title: DecorApp Research And Positioning
recaps.summary: This past hour I kicked off research for the decor app, the next app in the series. The script is written for someone who's new to the channel, so it explains each piece in plain terms as it comes up. It starts with why I do research before building anything. Then it covers what Claude is, what a skill is in practice (a research recipe I wrote once that gives every research doc the same shape), and what the HTML worker reviewer page at localhost:7778 is: a local page that turns Claude's write-up into a readable doc I can comment on directly. From there it goes through the research in order. First the problem. Then what already exists: the decor apps and chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini, and where all of them fall short. Then new idea concepts, each with its USP against the apps, its USP against the chatbots, and a viral feature. Then positioning: the target audience, the build options I weighed, and the chosen idea's USP and viral feature. It ends with a conclusion that brings the audience, the idea and why it wins together in one paragraph. Each part includes one decision I made and why. That finishes the research. Next step is turning it into the v1 build plan for the decor app.

lines.say: Hey folks, if you're new here, welcome. I'm building a series of real apps, one at a time, and I'm showing you my whole process as I go. The next app is a decor app, something to help people figure out how to decorate their space. Before I write any code for an app, I always do research first. I want to know what problem I'm solving, who's already solving it, and where there's actually room for something new. That's what I did this past hour, so let me walk you through how it works and what came out of it.

First, the tools, because this is probably your first time seeing them. I do a lot of this work with Claude, an AI assistant that I talk to in my terminal. For research I don't just type a random question into it. I use something I've built called a research skill. Think of it as a recipe. I wrote down once what a good research doc for this series looks like: the problem, what already exists, new ideas all judged the same way, who we're building for, and a conclusion. Every time I start research, Claude follows that recipe. That's my first decision, and here's why: if every app's research has the same shape, I can compare them, and I'm not hoping Claude invents a good structure on the fly.

This is what came back, and this page is the second tool. I call it the HTML worker reviewer. It's a small page that runs on my own machine. It takes what Claude wrote and shows it as a clean, readable document with a menu on the side, not a wall of raw text. The best part is that I can highlight any section, leave a comment on it, and Claude revises that part. That's the second decision: I review research here instead of reading raw text. It lets me read like an editor, point at the exact thing I want changed, and skip copying text back and forth into the chat.

So let's go through the research itself, top to bottom. It opens with the problem: what people actually struggle with when they try to decorate a room. Everything else in the doc gets checked against this section, so if an idea doesn't solve this problem, it doesn't make the cut.

Next is what already exists today. This covers the decor apps already out there, and also chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini. That's the third decision: I count chatbots as real competition, not just other apps. A lot of people now just open ChatGPT and ask 'how should I decorate my living room?' If I ignore that, everything I decide later has a blind spot. The research is honest about it, too. It found that ChatGPT and Gemini can already keep your room in mind and find real products. So I can't just claim we do that and they don't.

lines.act: localhost:7778, what they all miss section
lines.say: Then it lays out where all of them fall short, the apps and the chatbots. This is the gap we're aiming at. If there were no gap here, there'd be no reason to build this app.

Now for the fun part: new idea concepts for what we could build. Look at any one of these idea cards and you'll see the same three things on it. First, its USP against the existing apps. USP just means what makes it different, the reason someone would pick it. Second, its USP against the chatbots. Third, a viral feature, something that makes people want to share it. That's the fourth decision: every idea has to answer the same three questions. That way I'm judging them fairly, side by side, and not just picking whichever one sounds coolest right now.

lines.act: localhost:7778, decide what we build section
lines.say: After the ideas, the doc moves to deciding what we actually build. It starts with the target audience, who this is really for, and then lays out the build options I weighed. That's the fifth decision: I kept the options I didn't pick in the doc, not just the winner. Showing what I passed on, and why, proves the choice was thought through and not just a gut call. Then for the idea I chose, its USP and its viral feature are spelled out one more time so they're clear.

And it ends with the conclusion: one paragraph that brings together who it's for, what we're building, and why it wins. That's the sixth decision: the whole thing has to fit in one paragraph. My rule is that if I can't explain the idea in one breath, it isn't sharp enough to build yet.

So that's the research for the decor app, and I'm really happy with it. To recap: I gave Claude a research skill, basically my recipe for a research doc. It came back with a full write-up, and I reviewed it in the HTML worker page, leaving comments until it was right. We went from the problem, to who's solving it today, to the gap, to new ideas, to picking one, to a conclusion that fits in one paragraph. Next up, I'm turning this into the actual v1 build plan for the decor app. See you in the next one.

recaps.title: Positioning Skill For App_1
recaps.summary: This hour I built out positioning as a proper skill for app_1, the interior decor app, so it runs through html-worker the same way research already does and I can review it on a page and leave comments. I kept getting stuck on explaining why positioning even matters, so I pushed until we landed on the real reason: people only understand something new by comparing it to what they already know, so the doc uses other company names to anchor the pitch, and I got that reasoning written into both the skill and the review page. I also gave app_1 its own CLAUDE.md so app-specific facts stop cluttering the series-wide doc. Then I caught a real bug: the app progress visualizer wasn't showing app_1 as in-progress on positioning at all, so I fixed its scan to check for a positioning.md file, a named USP and viral feature, and the anchored-to comparison block. I restarted the visualizer through the monitoring center, and it now correctly shows app_1 at Stage 2, set up plus positioning, in progress. Next step is actually finishing the positioning doc so those checks turn green.

lines.say: Hey folks, so this stretch was all about positioning for app_1, the interior decor app, and turning it into something I can actually reuse.

So the first thing I did was turn positioning into its own skill, the same way research already works — it runs through html-worker so I get a page like this, I can leave comments, and it feeds back into how positioning runs next time.

But I kept getting stuck on why this step even matters, so I pushed on that — the point is people only understand something new by comparing it to what they already know, so this doc leans on other company names to anchor the pitch, and I added that reasoning right into the skill and the page itself.
I also wrote app_1's own CLAUDE.md so the app carries its own facts instead of cluttering the series-wide doc, which is where positioning decisions for this app now live.
Then I noticed something dumb — the app progress visualizer wasn't showing positioning as in progress for app_1 at all, even though I was clearly mid-way through it.
So I fixed the scan — it now checks for a positioning.md file, a named USP and viral feature, and that anchored-to comparison block, and all three go green once I actually save the doc.
Restarted it through the monitoring center like always, and now it correctly shows app_1 sitting at stage two, set up plus positioning, in progress.
Next up is finishing that positioning doc for real so those checks flip green, then it's on to actually building app_1.
